blocks.html: Data is a collection of raw facts and figures, such as numbers, words, measurements or observations. On its own, data may not mean much. For example, 85, 92, 67 are just numbers.
When data is processed (organised, calculated, compared), it becomes information that helps us make decisions: "The class average is 81, and Priya is the topper with 92."

blocks.html: Why data matters: schools use it to find weak subjects, hospitals to plan staff, banks to detect fraud, governments to plan schemes (the Census), and companies like Amazon and Flipkart to recommend products.

rows: Organised in rows and columns with a fixed format
Marksheet, railway reservation chart, bank statement
Photos, videos, voice notes, WhatsApp chats, emails
Harder; needs special tools such as AI

blocks.html: Semi-structured data sits in between. It has some labels but no fixed table shape, for example a JSON or XML file, or an email with a subject, sender and free text.

items.html: Qualitative (categorical) data describes a quality or category: gender, blood group, city, favourite subject, grade (A, B, C).
Quantitative (numerical) data is a measurable number:
Discrete: counted in whole numbers, such as the number of students in a class, goals in a match, or patients per day.
Continuous: measured, so it can take any value in a range, such as height (162.5 cm), weight, temperature or time.

blocks.html: Data collection means gathering data from the right sources for a purpose.

blocks.html: Ways to collect data: questionnaires and surveys, interviews, observation, sensors and IoT devices, website and app logs, and online forms.
Collected data must be stored safely so that it can be used later.

items.html: Storage devices: hard disk (HDD), solid state drive (SSD), pen drive, memory card.
Storage formats: text files and CSV files (Chapter 2), spreadsheets, databases (Chapters 8 and 9).
Cloud storage: Google Drive, OneDrive, and DigiLocker for documents. Data is kept on remote servers and can be reached from anywhere.

blocks.html: Units of storage: 1 byte = 8 bits · 1 KB = 1024 bytes · 1 MB = 1024 KB · 1 GB = 1024 MB · 1 TB = 1024 GB · 1 PB = 1024 TB.
Data processing turns raw data into information. The usual steps:

items.html: Collection: gather the data.
Preparation (cleaning): remove errors, duplicates and missing values.
Input: enter the data into the computer.
Processing: sort, search, calculate, compare and summarise (Chapters 5 and 6).
Output: present the results as tables, charts or reports.
Storage: save the data and the results for later use.

items.html: If n is odd, the median is the middle value, at position (n + 1) / 2.
If n is even, the median is the average of the two middle values.

blocks.html: Here n = 10 (even), so the middle values are the 5th and 6th: 67 and 67. The median = (67 +
67) / 2 = 67.
67 appears 3 times, more often than any other value, so the mode = 67. A data set can have no mode (all values appear once) or more than one mode.

blocks.html: Outlier example: salaries at a small company are ₹15,000, ₹18,000, ₹20,000, ₹22,000 and the owner's ₹5,00,000. The mean is ₹1,15,000, which describes no one. The median, ₹20,000, describes a typical employee much better.
Two classes can have the same mean but very different spreads. Class A scores 68, 70, 70, 72 and class B scores 40, 60, 80, 100. Both have a mean of 70, but class B is far more spread out.
For our data: 90 − 45 = 45.
(b) Standard deviation (σ) measures how far the values are from the mean, on average.
A small standard deviation means the marks are close to the mean (a consistent class). A large one means they are widely spread.

Note: this formula divides by n and is called the population standard deviation. When the data is only a sample of a bigger group, statisticians divide by n − 1 instead (the sample standard deviation). This book uses division by n unless stated otherwise.

items.html: Data is raw facts. Processing turns data into information that supports decisions.
Structured data fits rows and columns. Unstructured data (photos, videos, chats) has no fixed format. Semi-structured data (JSON, email) is in between.
Qualitative data describes categories. Quantitative data is numbers, either discrete (counted) or continuous (measured).
Primary data is collected first-hand. Secondary data was collected by others (Census, data.gov.in).
Data is stored on devices, in files and databases, and in the cloud. Processing runs from collection and cleaning through to output and storage.
Mean = sum / n. Median = middle of the sorted data. Mode = most frequent value.
Range = max − min. Standard deviation shows how spread out the values are around the mean.
The median is robust: outliers hardly change it, while they pull the mean.
In C++: accumulate , sort , minmax_element , map for frequencies, sqrt and pow .
